The paper presents a new, open-source numerical tool to compute Brownian thermal noise in amorphous and crystalline thin coatings for gravitational-wave detectors.
The tool uses a finite-element method, adaptive mesh refinement, and parallel processing to accurately resolve the thin coating layer.
Thermal noise is expected to be one of the key noise sources limiting the sensitivity of second-generation gravitational-wave detectors like Advanced LIGO and future third-generation detectors.
The paper focuses on modeling a cylindrical mirror with a single-layer, thin, reflective coating, with dimensions and properties similar to those considered in a previous experimental study.
The paper verifies the numerical convergence of the tool, estimating the numerical uncertainty in the coating energy to be around 0.1%.
For amorphous coatings, the numerical results agree well with approximate analytic solutions, capturing effects of edge boundaries and coating thickness.
Treating the crystalline AlGaAs coating as a cubic crystal increases the thermal noise by about 3% compared to modeling it as an effective isotropic material.
The paper's numerical calculations differ from an approximate analytic solution for an amorphous, semi-infinite mirror with a thin coating by around 4%.
The tool's computational time scales well with the number of compute cores used, with 50-100 cores providing a significant performance improvement.
Using hundreds of cores enables reaching higher resolutions by increasing the total available memory for the calculation.
Thermal noise is also a limiting factor in applications beyond gravitational-wave detectors, such as atomic clocks.
The paper's primary motivation is to help understand and reduce thermal noise in order to increase the sensitivity and reach of future gravitational-wave detectors.
The paper notes that while the tool is currently limited to single-layer coatings, future work will consider multi-layer coatings.
Experimental measurements of separate loss angles for the bulk and shear moduli of crystalline materials are still needed to fully model their thermal noise.
The paper's numerical tool is based on existing open-source frameworks, including deal.ii and PETSc, making it accessible for further development and use by the community.
